correspondence.component_scope: selected western opening
correspondence.finding: The atlas depicts the western Punta Gorda drainage turning south and then east into the main valley. The opening-detail imagery shows the corresponding vegetated drainage corridor within the same hill-and-clearing setting. The selected opening belongs to this continuous depicted route; individual canopy-obscured wetted threads are not required to be visible.
correspondence.name_scope: No separate headward reach name assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: upper eastward mainstem
correspondence.finding: Map5 continuously traces the western hook and eastward valley below Las Delicias, then the intermediate bends and receiving tributary junctions. Its Punta Gorda label lies on the same main drainage, rather than on a nearby parallel river. Overview and western-detail imagery corroborate the corresponding river-valley course.
correspondence.name_scope: Named main-river corridor; no independent scalar assignment to every tiny headward segment.

correspondence.component_scope: middle bends and fragment join
correspondence.finding: The atlas follows the main river eastward and northward through its middle bends and tributary-receiving setting before the lower southeastward course. The overview and lower-detail imagery show the corresponding broad river valley through the shared fragment join. The stored boundary is not treated as a separate watercourse or name change.
correspondence.name_scope: Same receiving main-river identity through the stored-fragment boundary.

correspondence.component_scope: lower southward valley
correspondence.finding: The river turns south through a sinuous valley before bending east across the coastal lowland. This configuration is continuously drawn on Map5 and independently visible in lower-detail imagery, including the lower receiving-junction setting. No unselected tributary is added to the naming candidate.
correspondence.name_scope: Lower main-river reach.

correspondence.component_scope: coastal wetland through passage
correspondence.finding: The lower eastward channel remains continuously mapped and visible through the vegetated coastal lowland and terminal meanders. The atlas describes the regional continental-to-littoral setting as low relief and predominantly wetland. No lake, reservoir, glacier, engineered canal or managed impoundment passage is required by this selected corridor at the inspected scale.
correspondence.name_scope: River passing through coastal wetland, not a name assigned to the wetland itself.

correspondence.component_scope: actual caribbean terminal
correspondence.finding: Map5 takes the named Punta Gorda channel directly to the Caribbean shoreline. The lower-detail image shows the same final meanders, widened mouth and open sea beyond the coastal edge. Both the source-ending reach and short rendered coastal extension are within this same mouth-to-sea receiving setting; no additional lake or alongshore outlet needs to be inferred.
correspondence.name_scope: Receiving sea, not a river alias.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen small Campo Alegre headward opening
correspondence.finding: The short headward line and its westward continuation lie in the mapped small-stream setting on the southern Campo Alegre side. The source drainage continues southwest into the named Vermelho/Humboldt channel. A separate scalar hydronym for the initial small feeder is not established.

correspondence.component_scope: Rio Vermelho / upper Humboldt corridor, including managed passage
correspondence.finding: The selected route follows the mapped channel south through the Rio Vermelho locality and forested protection-area valley. Municipal cartography uses Rio Humboldt ou Vermelho for the upper river; the operator’s own account places small hydropower installations on Rio Vermelho. The image depicts the local impounded/engineered river setting and continued descending valley. No new river, reservoir name or hydraulic separation is inferred from plant works.

correspondence.component_scope: Humboldt and Rio Natal convergence to the Rio Novo/Itapocu join
correspondence.finding: The selected southeastward descent follows Humboldt through the Rio Natal drainage convergence into Corupá. Detailed municipal cartography and AMVALI prose establish the connection to Rio Novo and the eastward receiving Rio Itapocu. Rio Natal and Rio Novo are joining rivers, not aliases assigned to the whole selection.

correspondence.component_scope: Itapocu from Corupá through Jaraguá do Sul
correspondence.finding: The source maps continue the same eastward then southeastward valley into Jaraguá do Sul and the Jaraguá tributary convergence. The stage3 model remains a single generalized mainstem across this named reach; no point-by-point bank agreement is required.

correspondence.component_scope: Guaramirim lowland and connected trunk bends
correspondence.finding: The river continues east through Guaramirim, receiving the mapped tributary network including the Itapocuzinho context, then turns through the broader lowland bends along the Araquari and São João do Itaperiú setting. The selected through-river is distinguished from tributary branches and nearby floodplain drains.

correspondence.component_scope: Araquari lower river and turn toward Barra Velha
correspondence.finding: Regional and municipal cartography, joined by the lower imagery view, account for the broad eastward meanders and subsequent southward turn through the lower floodplain and bridge corridor. All intermediate selected joins remain in the same river/receiving setting. Nearby oxbows and extraction ponds are not treated as route connectors or aliases.

correspondence.component_scope: Terminal Itapocu estuary and Atlantic opening
correspondence.finding: The final south-to-northeast bend follows the named Itapocu estuary on the Araquari–Barra Velha boundary into its actual open Atlantic outlet. The adjacent north/south coastal lagoon arms remain distinct; the selected endpoint is not replaced with a nearby lagoon or the Babitonga system farther north.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen northern opening and Hicks Station Wash
correspondence.finding: The regional original depicts the chosen opening in the same north-south valley drainage that is labeled Hicks Station Wash. The upper detail identifies the wash beside Hicks Spring and follows its southward valley bend around the western side of the Park Range. The broader original supplies minor headward linework that is less visible in the detailed display. This is the selected valley opening, not a nearby spring or an unselected mountain tributary substituted for it.
correspondence.name_scope: Hicks Station Wash is the bounded upper reach; Hicks Spring is a neighboring point feature, not an alternative river name.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper wash continuation and entry into the broader Hot Creek Valley
correspondence.finding: The selected southward continuation remains on the mapped axial wash through the Pritchards Station surroundings, west of the Rhyolite Hills and Needle Range. Side washes and the axial continuation are continuously depicted in the overview, while the detail shows the same valley passage and drainage joins. No lake, mountain divide or lateral interbasin transfer is needed for this link.
correspondence.name_scope: The upper named wash continues toward the differently named middle collector; an exact hydronym-change point is not asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Moores Station Wash middle collector
correspondence.finding: The broader valley corridor is repeatedly labeled Moores Station Wash on the middle original. The selected southwestward bend follows that same drainage west of Halligan Mesa toward the Hot Creek junction. The surrounding dry tributary fans are ordinary parts of this mapped collecting corridor; present surface flow is not required.
correspondence.name_scope: Moores Station Wash is a distinct selected middle reach, not an alias of Hicks Station Wash or Hot Creek.

correspondence.component_scope: Moores Station Wash–Hot Creek join, Tybo junction and U.S. Highway 6 crossing
correspondence.finding: The middle original explicitly depicts Moores Station Wash joining Hot Creek from the north, followed by the Tybo Creek junction and a southeastward Hot Creek continuation across U.S. Highway 6. The selected route uses the northern collector and then the receiving Hot Creek trunk; it does not follow the western Hot Creek headwaters or Tybo Creek. Rush and Everett independently describe a northern main tributary joining Hot Creek in midvalley.
correspondence.name_scope: Hot Creek is the receiving trunk and representative system identity. Tybo Creek and the western Hot Creek headwater reach are unselected tributary context.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Hot Creek valley and shallow-water/slough approach
correspondence.finding: The regional and lower originals continuously depict the selected lower Hot Creek corridor beside the western foot of the Pancake Range, including the small water patches before the State Route 375 bend. The channel passes through this lowland into the canyon/slough approach. No selected reservoir crossing or separate canal-system transfer is established or needed.
correspondence.name_scope: The receiving creek remains Hot Creek; the small water patches are not independently named.

correspondence.component_scope: Twin Springs Slough and the Pancake Range outlet
correspondence.finding: The selected southeastward passage corresponds to the water-bearing corridor labeled Twin Springs Slough beside State Route 375 and continues through the narrow opening into Railroad Valley. The 1966 report explicitly describes Hot Creek leaving Hot Creek Valley at Twin Springs Ranch through a narrow Pancake Range canyon. Its historical irrigation remarks provide context only and are not used to infer present diversions or operating conditions.
correspondence.name_scope: Twin Springs Slough is a distinct named passage within the receiving system, not a whole-system alias.

correspondence.component_scope: Southern outlet fan and minor-pan chain
correspondence.finding: Downstream of the canyon, the originals depict an east-northeast branch labeled Hot Creek and a separate southward drainage continuation beside State Route 375 into a chain of small pans and the northern margin of the terminal playa. The selected southern course stays within this continuously mapped low receiving floor. Cartographic drainage and the enclosing lowland establish fan-to-playa correspondence at ordinary scale; neither an exact wet thread nor a present-day transfer between individual shallow pans is asserted. The mapped eastern Hot Creek branch is not substituted for the selected southern ending.
correspondence.name_scope: The southern fan/pan continuation has no independently established reach name; Hot Creek is retained only as the representative receiving-system identity.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual unnamed Railroad Valley playa terminal
correspondence.finding: The selected final continuation enters the northern side of the large playa east of State Route 375 and ends within its mapped floor. This is the same receiving floor approached from the outlet fan, without an intervening ridge or a separate selected basin crossing at the examined scale. The DOE rail assessment independently places this playa in Railroad Valley and describes nearby washes terminating in it; that context does not replace the topographic evidence for the selected northern approach.
correspondence.name_scope: The terminal playa name is unconfirmed and remains null. Railroad Valley is a regional valley label, not a newly assigned lake name.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen Budd Lake opening and upper South Branch to Bartley
correspondence.finding: The selected opening lies in the southwestern Budd Lake setting. The detailed original depicts the lake, its southwestern outlet under the road corridor and the connected South Branch Raritan River running south and southeast through the wooded valley to Bartley. Repeated river labels distinguish this outlet route from nearby lake feeders and Mine Brook. The entire chosen opening and collecting corridor are established without assigning exact banks or a hydronym boundary.
correspondence.name_scope: Budd Lake is the initial lake; South Branch Raritan River is the distinct downstream branch name.

correspondence.component_scope: Drakes Brook junction, Long Valley and Middle Valley
correspondence.finding: Original cartography depicts Drakes Brook arriving from the east near the Bartley–Four Bridges setting and joining the South Branch, which continues southwest through Naughright and Long Valley toward Middle Valley. Electric Brook meets the river at Long Valley. The selected parts remain in this continuously mapped receiving valley; the branch is not renamed after its tributaries.
correspondence.name_scope: South Branch Raritan River, with Drakes Brook and Electric Brook as separate tributary joins.

correspondence.component_scope: Califon, narrow valley, Lake Solitude and High Bridge
correspondence.finding: The upper-middle original continuously depicts the South Branch south from Middle Valley through Califon and the constricted river valley to Readingsburg, into Lake Solitude and out through High Bridge. The lake passage and downstream outlet are visible on the original and an enlarged local reading. The same river continues toward the northern Clinton approach. No present dam operation or exact shoreline is inferred.
correspondence.name_scope: South Branch Raritan River is the named branch; Lake Solitude is a separate through-lake component.

correspondence.component_scope: Clinton tributary joins and Hamden corridor
correspondence.finding: The South Branch passes Clinton and continues south through the Landsdown–Hamden corridor. The map shows Spruce Run arriving from its separate reservoir to the west, Beaver Brook entering from the east, and Cakepoulin Creek meeting the river farther south. The NJWSA authorial configuration and system schematic independently distinguish the Spruce Run inflow and off-line Round Valley storage from the selected South Branch. The selected path does not pass through either large reservoir.
correspondence.name_scope: South Branch Raritan River; Spruce Run, Beaver Brook and Cakepoulin Creek remain separate tributaries. Spruce Run Reservoir and Round Valley Reservoir are contextual water-supply components, not river aliases.

correspondence.component_scope: Stanton, Flemington Junction, Three Bridges and Neshanic turn
correspondence.finding: The original maps the South Branch past Stanton and the Rowland Mills–Flemington Junction corridor, then east past Three Bridges and Neshanic Station before its northward turn. The Neshanic River enters this southern South Branch reach; the NJWSA river-configuration prose confirms that join lies upstream of the North Branch confluence. The selected path stays in the depicted river corridor throughout the bend and northward continuation.
correspondence.name_scope: South Branch Raritan River; Neshanic River is a distinct joining tributary.

correspondence.component_scope: North Branch junction, Raritan river corridor and water-power canal setting
correspondence.finding: The map depicts the South Branch reaching the North Branch from the southwest; their receiving Raritan River continues east through the Duke Island–Raritan setting. Holland Brook joins the South Branch near this approach. The Raritan Water Power Canal is separately labeled along the northern side of the connected river corridor. Original river and canal linework establish the shared corridor and connected junctions; the generalized selection is not used to assign every position to an exact channel or canal bank.
correspondence.name_scope: Raritan River is the receiving mainstem and representative system identity; North Branch Raritan River and Raritan Water Power Canal are separate components.

correspondence.component_scope: Somerville–Manville, Millstone junction and Bound Brook
correspondence.finding: The original depicts the Raritan east past the Somerville–Manville corridor, receiving the Millstone River from the south and continuing toward Bound Brook. The mapped Delaware and Raritan Canal runs separately beside the Millstone and lower Raritan. NJWSA configuration prose and Figure 2 confirm the Millstone join and distinguish river intakes, canal releases and the canal terminus. These managed connections provide context; no unselected canal journey or reservoir transfer is substituted for the selected receiving-river corridor.
correspondence.name_scope: Raritan River, distinct Millstone River tributary and separately named Delaware and Raritan Canal.

correspondence.component_scope: Bound Brook bend, Fieldville and New Brunswick approach
correspondence.finding: The mapped Raritan turns south beside South Bound Brook, passes Fieldville and continues southeast toward New Brunswick. The adjoining canal remains distinguishable beside the river, and the river is continuously mapped through the bridge corridors. This is an established connected river setting rather than an unresolved transfer between watersheds.
correspondence.name_scope: Raritan River; the adjoining Delaware and Raritan Canal is not a synonym.

correspondence.component_scope: New Brunswick, Lawrence Brook join and upper tidal meanders
correspondence.finding: The terminal original shows the widening Raritan downstream of New Brunswick, past the Lawrence Brook mouth and through the island-bearing tidal meanders eastward. Lawrence Brook and the smaller shore creeks remain separate tributaries. All selected intervals fall within the continuously depicted lower-river corridor; individual tidal subchannels and present inundation are not assigned.
correspondence.name_scope: Lower Raritan River and distinct tributary mouths.

correspondence.component_scope: South River mouth, Crab Island reach and actual estuarine ending
correspondence.finding: The lower original depicts the South River joining the Raritan estuarine corridor near Sayreville, the connected waters around Crab Island and the widening lower river through the major bridge crossings toward Perth Amboy and South Amboy. The actual rendered ending lies in this same broad Raritan mouth-water setting, immediately upstream of its opening to the bay. NJWSA Figure 2 identifies the receiving Raritan River and Bay system. No selected cross-watershed transfer or unexplained inland terminal remains. The two supplied terminal descriptors are retained as distinct source and rendered endpoints; neither is silently replaced by a more easterly coastal point.
correspondence.name_scope: Raritan River estuary; South River is a joining tributary and Raritan Bay is the receiving coastal setting, not a river alias.
